title: Drug-free donor-specific tolerance for pediatric solid-organ grafts

concept.text: The proposed innovation is durable immune acceptance of a transplanted organ in a child, allowing all maintenance anti-rejection drugs to stop. Donor-specific tolerance means accepting tissue from that particular donor while retaining useful immune responses against other targets. The intended scope includes clinically relevant kidney, liver, heart, lung and intestinal grafts, including HLA-mismatched donors, rather than depending on a closely matched sibling donor.

The target capability would work without requiring radiation or other genotoxic conditioning and without causing graft-versus-host disease, in which transferred donor immune cells attack the recipient. A one-time intervention is the envisioned treatment model, but its sufficiency remains part of the proposal. In children, acceptance would need to remain durable as the recipient grows and the immune system develops. Complete drug withdrawal is central: removing steroids while continuing other anti-rejection medicines would represent a different outcome.

significance.text: Conditional impact: successful drug-free graft acceptance would remove the daily maintenance anti-rejection treatment burden during the period for which tolerance was demonstrated. For a child facing decades of life after transplantation, sustained freedom from that treatment could substantially change the experience of living with a graft. Stable graft function through observed growth, without rejection or graft-versus-host disease, would be the direct benefit sought.

Further benefits would depend on what the intervention actually prevents and what risks it introduces. The research identifies infection, cancer and impaired growth as concerns associated with pediatric transplantation and immunosuppression, but the supplied review could not verify their frequency or causal attribution. Reducing immunosuppressive exposure could reduce some treatment-related harms; it would not establish that all such complications disappear, especially if the tolerance procedure itself carries significant risks.

Calling the result a lifelong cure would go beyond the proposed evidence. Donor-specific tolerance addresses immune acceptance; it does not by itself eliminate every cause of graft dysfunction or establish lifelong graft survival. Likewise, the basic immune goal is shared with adult transplantation. HLA mismatch, thoracic organs and deceased-donor applicability are broader transplant challenges, while durability during growth supplies a specifically pediatric requirement.

missing_breakthrough.text: The capability sought is a reliable way to establish and maintain donor-specific tolerance across clinically relevant pediatric recipients and organs, with complete withdrawal of maintenance immunosuppression. Evidence confined to adult HLA-matched sibling kidney recipients, if confirmed, would demonstrate a narrower achievement. The supplied material does not establish how widely the broader pediatric capability remains unmet or quantify children's access to matched sibling donors.

Engineering synthesis: the protocol must solve several linked problems—establish sufficient acceptance across HLA differences, sustain it after drugs stop, and preserve useful immune function. If donor immune cells are part of the approach, graft-versus-host disease must be avoided. If preparation of the recipient is necessary, the protocol must achieve its effect without requiring radiation or other genotoxic conditioning. The reported adult outcomes cannot resolve these constraints because the retained material does not establish the treatment or conditioning details.

Engineering synthesis: extending an approach across organs requires evidence that tolerance protects each graft type, rather than assuming that a kidney result transfers to heart, lung, liver or intestine. Pediatric durability adds the need to observe recipients through continued growth. Deceased-donor use adds a practical requirement: donor material, preparation and treatment timing must fit that setting. These are requirements of the proposed capability, not barriers shown to have been solved by the supplied reports.

current_state.text: The research attributes to Kaufman and colleagues a 2025 American Journal of Transplantation phase 3 trial of the donor-cell product MDR-101 in living-related HLA-matched kidney recipients, identified by DOI 10.1016/j.ajt.2025.01.044. It reports that 15 of 20 treated patients, or 75%, remained immunosuppression-free for more than two years, with no death, graft loss, donor-specific antibody or graft-versus-host disease in the treated arm. These quantitative findings are preserved as attributed results: the supplied source index contains no retained article text or artifacts, so the review could not verify the trial phase, population, treatment, outcome definitions or follow-up details.

An accompanying editorial dated 21 February 2025 is described in the research as identifying the recipients as adults receiving kidneys from two-haplotype HLA-matched siblings. That population description also remains unverified because no editorial text was retained. If both descriptions are confirmed, the trial would support sustained drug-free graft acceptance in a restricted adult kidney population. It would not establish pediatric efficacy, applicability to mismatched or thoracic grafts, or compliance with the proposed restriction on genotoxic conditioning. The reported two-year outcome also would not establish lifelong tolerance.

A separate August 2025 abstract is described as reporting complete immunosuppression withdrawal in two of six haplotype-matched recipients. The research does not identify these recipients as children. No abstract text was retained, leaving the matching terminology, recipient ages, protocol, duration of withdrawal and safety outcomes unresolved. This remains an attributed abstract-level result; it cannot establish pediatric tolerance or the broader proposed capability.

The research also cites pediatric analyses of steroid-free regimens and describes children as continuing other immunosuppression. If confirmed, those findings concern reduced drug burden rather than complete drug-free donor-specific tolerance. The distinction matters even when steroid avoidance is clinically useful. The source text was not retained, so the review could not establish the exact regimens, populations or outcomes.

Evidence boundary: all four supplied source records contain bibliographic URLs but no captured source texts or artifacts. This prevents independent verification within this record; it is not evidence that the attributed results are false. The supplied bounded search record is also empty. Consequently, the dated 2025 reports can be described with their uncertainties, but the material does not establish whether the broader pediatric target remains unavailable as of 1 November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: a prospective pediatric study would use a defined protocol without required radiation or other genotoxic conditioning, include HLA-mismatched grafts and at least one thoracic organ, and achieve complete withdrawal of maintenance immunosuppression. Successful recipients would maintain stable graft function without donor-specific antibody, rejection or graft-versus-host disease for a prespecified multi-year period that includes continued body growth. These are proposed criteria, not established consensus thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Multi-year drug-free graft acceptance maintained through continued pediatric growth

completion_criteria.text: Proposed assessment: the study would define withdrawal timing, surveillance methods, graft-function measures and rules for restarting treatment before evaluating success. It would report all enrolled recipients, including those who could not withdraw drugs, those who needed treatment restarted and those with serious adverse outcomes. This would distinguish the chance of achieving drug-free acceptance from its durability among selected responders. Steroid freedom while tacrolimus, mycophenolate or another maintenance anti-rejection drug continues would not meet the proposed endpoint.
completion_criteria.label: Prespecified withdrawal criteria and outcomes reported for all recipients

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and scope: independent teams would reproduce the result using a sufficiently specified protocol and report outcomes separately by organ, HLA relationship, recipient age and donor setting. A further field-level demonstration would extend the protocol to deceased donors under workable procurement and treatment timelines. Evidence in one thoracic organ would establish experience in that organ, not automatically in every other graft type.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication with specified protocols and separately reported subgroup outcomes

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: convincing success would require acceptable overall treatment risk, including the initial intervention, and evidence that useful immune function is preserved. Follow-up should describe the growth and developmental stages actually observed. Multi-year success would demonstrate durability over that interval; even reproducible results across several cohorts would establish demonstrated breadth rather than literal universality or lifelong protection.
completion_criteria.label: Acceptable overall treatment risk with preserved useful immune function

related_concepts.text: PED-13, Drug-free reset of severe pediatric autoimmune disease, is the closest conceptual overlap. Both seek durable immune reprogramming that removes the need for chronic immune suppression. Their targets differ: PED-12 seeks acceptance of donor tissue, whereas PED-13 concerns harmful immune responses against the child's own tissues. A successful mechanism in one setting would not establish success in the other.

PED-02, Protective adaptive immunity generated by the newborn, shares an interest in immune development but seeks a different capability. PED-02 aims to generate protective responses; PED-12 aims to establish selective acceptance while retaining useful immunity. This distinction makes preservation of protective immune function an important proposed boundary for transplantation tolerance.

PED-07, A physiological subpulmonary ventricle for single-ventricle heart disease, and PED-08, Restoration of nephron endowment after the nephrogenic clock stops, address organ function through different routes. Their roster titles concern creating or restoring physiological capacity; PED-12 concerns immune acceptance of an organ supplied by a donor. Successful organ restoration might alter transplant needs for some patients, but it would not demonstrate transplant tolerance.

PED-06, Prenatal correction that lets severe monogenic disease develop normally, and PED-11, One-time in vivo correction of severe newborn metabolic disease before irreversible injury, share the ambition of an early intervention with durable benefit. Their proposed targets are disease-causing defects, whereas PED-12 targets the recipient's immune relationship with donor tissue. A common one-time-treatment ambition does not make their mechanisms or completion criteria interchangeable.

unresolved_issues: The four source URLs have no retained texts or artifacts. Article identities, publication details and attributed findings remain unverified within the supplied record.

The MDR-101 trial's conditioning regimen, eligibility criteria, withdrawal definitions, follow-up distribution and outcome ascertainment are unresolved. Its compatibility with the proposed conditioning constraint cannot be inferred.
The separate six-recipient abstract does not establish recipient ages, precise HLA relationships, withdrawal duration, protocol or safety outcomes in the supplied material.
The pediatric steroid-free analysis lacks retained evidence establishing its exact regimens, populations and outcomes.
No supplied evidence quantifies pediatric access to matched sibling donors or establishes the frequency and causes of the listed treatment complications.
The empty freshness record prevents a conclusion about the broader capability's availability as of 1 November 2026.

The proposed study duration, acceptable overall success rate, surveillance schedule, safety limits and breadth of independent replication remain to be specified; no numerical consensus thresholds are supplied.

brief.title: Organ transplants children can keep without daily drugs
possible: A child with a transplanted organ could stop all daily anti-rejection medicines while keeping the organ working as they grow. Their immune system would accept that donor’s tissue while still defending against other targets.

The goal covers kidneys, livers, hearts, lungs and intestines, including donors whose immune markers differ from the child’s. Treatment would avoid radiation, other preparation that damages DNA, and attacks on the child by transferred donor immune cells.
why: For children facing decades with a transplant, freedom from daily anti-rejection treatment would change everyday life. Sustained acceptance would let them grow with a functioning graft without the continuing burden of maintenance medicines.

sources.showed: A trial studied MDR-101, a donor-cell treatment, in kidney recipients with closely matched donor immune markers.
sources.cited_for: The trial reports sustained freedom from anti-rejection medicines in closely matched kidney recipients.
sources.not_established: It does not establish success in children, across other organs or donor mismatches, or without DNA-damaging preparation.

sources.showed: An editorial describes the trial recipients as adults receiving kidneys from siblings with closely matched immune markers.
sources.cited_for: It identifies the narrow adult population behind the reported kidney results.
sources.not_established: That population does not establish whether the treatment works in children or with less closely matched donors.

sources.who: Authors of the transplant withdrawal abstract
sources.showed: A conference abstract reports complete withdrawal of anti-rejection medicines in some recipients with partly matched donor immune markers.
sources.cited_for: It reports drug withdrawal beyond the closely matched sibling kidney trial.
sources.not_established: It does not establish pediatric success, lasting acceptance or the treatment’s safety.

sources.who: Authors of the pediatric steroid-free treatment analysis
sources.showed: A pediatric analysis examines treatment without steroids while children continue other anti-rejection medicines.
sources.cited_for: It supports the distinction between reducing medicines and stopping all maintenance anti-rejection treatment.
sources.not_established: Stopping steroids alone does not establish drug-free acceptance of a transplanted organ.

shown: Kaufman and colleagues report that some closely matched kidney recipients stayed off anti-rejection medicines for more than two years. An accompanying editorial identifies them as adults receiving sibling kidneys. This is the clearest reported advance toward sustained drug-free acceptance.
missing: Children would need to keep functioning grafts without maintenance drugs through continued growth, including with mismatched donors.
Treatment would need to avoid DNA-damaging preparation and donor immune cells attacking the child, while preserving useful immune defenses.
Success would need to extend across organ types and fit the timing and practical demands of deceased donation.

milestones.label: Drug-free graft acceptance lasts as children grow
milestones.explanation: A pediatric study would need lasting drug-free function across donor mismatches, including a heart or lung, without DNA-damaging preparation, rejection or donor-cell attacks. This would test acceptance through growth.

milestones.label: Withdrawal rules and every recipient’s outcome are reported
milestones.explanation: A study would need advance rules for stopping, monitoring and restarting medicines, and report every recipient’s outcome. This would reveal the chance of success, including people who cannot stop treatment.

milestones.label: Independent teams repeat results across recipient and donor groups
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would need to repeat a specified protocol, separate outcomes by organ, matching, age and donor setting, and extend it to deceased donors. This would establish reproducibility and practical reach.

milestones.label: Overall treatment risk is acceptable and immune defenses remain
milestones.explanation: Follow-up would need to show acceptable risk from the whole treatment and preserved immune defenses through observed development. This would establish whether drug-free acceptance delivers a worthwhile overall benefit.

uncertain: It remains unclear whether a single intervention can sustain donor-specific acceptance as a child’s immune system develops.
The adult trial’s compatibility with avoiding DNA-damaging preparation remains unresolved.
The required follow-up, acceptable success rate and safety limits still need definition; success over several years would not establish lifelong protection.

page.title: Donor-specific tolerance in pediatric solid-organ transplantation
page.definition: Children retain functioning organ grafts after all maintenance anti-rejection drugs stop, accepting the donor while retaining immunity to other targets as they grow. The capability includes donors with mismatched human leukocyte antigens, the proteins used for tissue matching, without DNA-damaging conditioning or graft-versus-host disease, in which donor immune cells attack the child.

goal.need: HRSA describes one to three anti-rejection medicines for most pediatric organ recipients. Among 923 Nordic liver recipients transplanted before age 30 during 1982–2013, 37 cancers occurred over 7,846 person-years; incidence was 9.8 times that in matched general populations. Complete withdrawal would remove maintenance treatment exposure. These cancer figures describe post-transplant risk, not the amount that drug withdrawal would prevent.

figures.caption: Cumulative cancer incidence after liver transplantation before age 30
figures.note: The Nordic cohort included children and young adults: 923 recipients transplanted during 1982–2013. Estimates account for the competing risk of death.

statements.quote: The ultimate goal of transplant immunosuppression is to induce immunologic tolerance, where maintenance immunosuppression can be discontinued
statements.context: From its PedSAP educational chapter on immunosuppression in pediatric solid-organ transplantation.

statements.quote: complete and planned withdrawal of all immunosuppression while maintaining the healthy function of the graft organ.
statements.context: The network identifies this as the primary goal of its interventional transplantation studies.

completion.title: Pediatric grafts achieve drug-free donor-specific tolerance across the five organ cases.
completion.criterion: For each organ case, a prospective pediatric study meets its registered endpoint for complete maintenance-immunosuppression withdrawal with normal or stable graft function, confirmed clinically, biochemically and histologically. Demonstrate donor-specific immune unresponsiveness with retained immunity to non-donor antigens during observed childhood growth. Include HLA-mismatched recipients, use no irradiation or other genotoxic conditioning, and observe no graft-versus-host disease. Follow-up duration and success proportion remain protocol-specific.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis; no outside body located defines this combined pediatric, cross-organ capability.
completion.basis: Searches of FDA/EMA guidance, NIAID/ITN programmes, the AST transplantation forum report and pediatric trial registries found no test combining all five organs, HLA mismatch, growth and non-genotoxic conditioning. This test combines ITN's graft-health and immunocompetence objectives with the forum's donor-specific functional criterion. No universal duration or success fraction is added. Published results establish narrower outcomes.

milestones.title: An animal organ graft survives drug-free while donor skin is accepted and unrelated skin is rejected.
milestones.criterion: After maintenance immunosuppression stops, retain the organ graft and accept a subsequent donor skin graft while rejecting third-party skin. This experimental challenge tests donor specificity rather than generalized immune suppression. Bashuda and colleagues reported long-term kidney survival in 3/6 treated rhesus monkeys, lasting 410–880 days at study end; a challenged long-term survivor retained donor skin while rejecting third-party skin by day 40.
milestones.set_by: Experimental transplantation convention, applied by Bashuda and colleagues in their nonhuman-primate kidney study; the published experiment concerned kidneys.
milestones.threshold_quote: third-party but not donor skin was rejected

milestones.title: A pediatric organ graft functions for at least one year without maintenance immunosuppression.
milestones.criterion: Remain off immunosuppression for at least one year with normal graft function. WISP-R reported this outcome in 12/20 selected pediatric liver recipients. Separately, the adult MDR-101 kidney trial reported more than two years off drugs in 15/20 treated recipients; its 30 participants received HLA-matched sibling kidneys, and treatment included lymphoid irradiation. A 2026 intestinal case reported a 12-year-old girl rejection-free for more than three years after withdrawal for lymphoproliferative disease, following graft-versus-host disease.
milestones.set_by: Immune Tolerance Network, WISP-R protocol ITN029ST, version 5.0, dated 19 April 2011; written for pediatric parental living-donor liver grafts.
milestones.threshold_quote: those who remain off immunosuppression for at least 1 year.

milestones.title: A pediatric organ graft passes biochemical and biopsy tests one year after complete drug withdrawal.
milestones.criterion: At one year after the last immunosuppressive dose, demonstrate stable graft function without rejection and no more than minimal biopsy change from the prewithdrawal biopsy. The iWITH liver-specific endpoint required alanine aminotransferase and gamma-glutamyl transferase below 50 U/L and the histological criteria in Supporting Table S1. Among 88 selected children, 33 met the endpoint, 16 failed histological criteria despite meeting biochemical criteria, and 39 failed because of rejection. The numerical liver limits are not validated for other organs.
milestones.set_by: Immune Tolerance Network and iWITH investigators, NCT01638559 primary efficacy endpoint; written for pediatric liver grafts.
milestones.threshold_quote: liver biopsy with no more than minimal change compared with the eligibility biopsy

milestones.title: A pediatric graft recipient shows donor-specific immune unresponsiveness with third-party responses.
milestones.criterion: Functional assays show unresponsiveness to the organ donor alongside recovered responses to unrelated donors. In the 2022 Schimke immuno-osseous dysplasia series, all three children showed donor-specific T-cell tolerance with responses to non-donor cells at least one year after kidney transplantation. Normal kidney function without immunosuppression persisted for 22–34 months. These children had pre-existing T-cell immunodeficiency and received conditioning that included total-body irradiation and cyclophosphamide.
milestones.set_by: Clinical transplantation convention described by Leventhal and Mathew in their account of the American Society of Transplantation Transplantation Research Forum; demonstrated in a pediatric kidney series.
milestones.threshold_quote: proof of donor-specific unresponsiveness with recovered third-party responses in functional assays in vitro

milestones.title: A pediatric organ graft retains function and stable histology through four years off immunosuppression.
milestones.criterion: Sustain operational tolerance—stable graft function and histology without immunosuppression—through the four-year postwithdrawal assessment used in WISP-R. Its 12-child liver extension reported no chronic rejection, graft loss or death and no progressive increase in inflammation or fibrosis. One participant withdrew consent 33.3 months after the one-year tolerance assessment. Four years off drugs is this study's observation interval, not a consensus cutoff or evidence of lifelong tolerance.
milestones.set_by: Immune Tolerance Network, WISP-R durability follow-up with biopsies two and four years after withdrawal; written for pediatric parental living-donor liver grafts.
milestones.threshold_quote: were followed for a total of five years (one year of IS withdrawal and four years off IS)

not_found: No published cross-organ pediatric completion threshold specifying follow-up duration, success proportion or tolerance through growth was located.
No prospective pediatric heart or lung cohort meeting the combined completion criteria was located.
The supplied editorial, haplotype-matched conference abstract and pediatric steroid-free analysis could not be opened at their publisher URLs.
The iWITH supplementary document containing the full histological scoring criteria could not be opened.
The 2026 intestinal report's indexed abstract was available, but its publisher full text could not be opened.
